mechanicalFacts: Forward torso lean is greater than standard. This is structurally necessary, not a form error.
Knee travel is more forward to keep the bar over mid-foot.
On the way up the hips rise first and the torso lags — the sticking point sits just above parallel.
Hip crease reaches parallel later in the descent arc.
stanceCue: Lifters with this structure typically find a stance slightly wider than hip-width, with toes turned out, keeps the knee path aligned with long femurs.
irrelevantCue: "Keep your torso upright" → With long femurs, an upright torso moves the bar forward of mid-foot. The lean is the solution, not the problem.

mechanicalFacts: Torso stays closer to upright through the descent — short femurs need less forward lean to keep the bar over mid-foot.
Knee travel forward is more pronounced relative to hip travel, since the shin does more of the work on a shorter thigh lever.
The sticking point on the way up is milder — less torso lag than a long-femur build.
Hip crease reaches parallel earlier in the descent arc than a long-femur build.
stanceCue: Lifters with this structure typically find a narrower stance suits the shorter thigh segment without excess knee travel.
irrelevantCue: "Sit back like you're reaching for a chair behind you" → With short femurs, an exaggerated hip-back setup shifts the bar in front of mid-foot and forces extra torso lean to compensate.

mechanicalFacts: Torso lean sits between the long- and short-femur extremes — a moderate forward angle keeps the bar over mid-foot.
Hip and knee flexion progress at a similar rate through the descent.
On the way up the hips lead slightly, so the torso pitches a little further forward through the sticking point.
Hip crease reaches parallel around the midpoint of the typical depth range.
stanceCue: A hip-width stance with toes turned out slightly is a common starting point for this balanced proportion.
irrelevantCue: "There's one correct squat depth for everyone" → Depth that keeps the bar over mid-foot without losing the neutral spine looks different even for a proportional build, depending on ankle and hip mobility.

mechanicalFacts: A wider hip relative to shoulder width changes how the knees track outward through the descent.
Setup width often needs to be wider than a narrower-hipped build to keep the knees aligned over the toes.
On the way up the hips lead into the sticking point the same as a proportional build, with a slightly wider knee path.
The bar path can still stay over mid-foot, but the knee-out angle needed to achieve it is naturally greater.
stanceCue: Lifters with this structure typically find a wider stance with more toe-out keeps the knees tracking in line with a wider hip.
irrelevantCue: "Keep your knees narrow, in line with hip-width feet" → With a wider hip structure, narrow knee tracking forces the femurs into an angle that isn't necessary — wider knee tracking is the natural fit, not a fault.
